title: Council Post: Maximize Productivity With AI-Powered Knowledge Management
text:
Sirjad Parakkat is the VP of Engineering for Ivanti, leading the IT Service Management, Lines of Business and Platinum Engineering Group.
Too much of a good thing? That’s what it feels like when discussing the current data and knowledge landscape. Every conceivable bit and byte of information is, quite literally, at our fingertips.
Many have said data is the new oil—those who produce, shape, control and own it are at a distinct power advantage. Information is currency. But having it isn’t enough.
How do you break away from the pack amid the current onslaught of data and corresponding knowledge?
You need to not only have information but also know how to use it wisely.
Effective Knowledge Management: A Critical Factor
Companies with effective knowledge management are more secure. They’re more efficient. Their employees are more productive, with less burnout and turnover. They can make better choices faster and with less effort. The list goes on.
The key to effective knowledge management may boil down to one rapidly evolving technology: AI.
AI-powered knowledge management can revolutionize how companies access, use and share knowledge across their workforce.
Why Traditional Knowledge Management Isn’t Enough
The rapid proliferation of data mentioned above becomes a severe problem when butting up against legacy knowledge management systems that simply aren’t equipped to handle so much input at one time.
Traditionally, companies may have gotten away with managing relevant information stored across multiple sources and systems. In legacy systems, it’s common for every department to maintain its own knowledge repository. At best, this siloed approach creates significant inefficiencies in accessing relevant data—but slowed processes are just the tip of the iceberg. Siloed information impedes cross-department collaboration and decision-making. It can hinder the visibility of security gaps and other business-critical information.
These systems can cause problems even without considering that the world is hurtling toward producing 200 zettabytes of data by 2025.
How AI Can Make A Difference
AI is not without detractors, and for good reason. For one thing, AI has become a powerful weapon for threat actors looking to elevate their cybercrime capabilities—among other concerns.
But AI is also becoming impressively adept at processing and managing vast quantities of information—to an extent that would have seemed unfathomable just a few years ago. To combat the challenges described above, AI-powered knowledge management can centralize information from disparate sources and leverage algorithms to streamline access and analysis. (It’s the anti-silo.)
For knowledge workers, this is big—and personalized, context-specific search makes it even better. Unlike traditional systems that rely on keyword-based searches, AI-powered platforms rely on natural language processing (NLP), semantic search and machine learning. Precise, personalized knowledge delivery is made possible based on an understanding of user context, preferences and behavior. That’s excellent for your marketing department looking to provide a more personalized experience for consumers, but it’s also a game-changer for all knowledge workers.
While standard, static knowledge repositories offer generic information to all users, AI-driven platforms can adapt dynamically to individual user needs, presenting relevant content in real time based on factors such as role, department and previous interactions. That means getting the right information faster than relying on universal keyword searches. Ultimately, this can lead to improvements in efficiency, productivity and the overall employee experience.
Five Steps To Implementing AI-Powered Knowledge Management
If you’ve been using the same approach to knowledge management for years or even decades, a shift of this magnitude can feel overwhelming. But the magnitude of the potential upside should convince business leaders that it’s worthy of consideration.
To help ensure success, take a strategic and systematic approach to adopting AI-powered knowledge management. Here are five key steps to get things started.
Identify specific challenges and opportunities: Every organization is different, and this isn’t the time for a one-size-fits-all approach. Start with a comprehensive assessment of existing knowledge management practices. To identify and prioritize areas for improvement, engage stakeholders across departments.
Define clear goals and objectives: What’s the aim? How will it be measured? Whether it's improving productivity, enhancing decision-making, elevating the employee experience or even taking a broader look and optimizing the customer experience, clearly define the desired outcomes to guide implementation efforts.
Choose the right AI technologies: Select AI technologies that align with the company’s knowledge management needs and objectives. Consider factors such as natural language processing, semantic search, machine learning and chatbots to enhance information retrieval, analysis and delivery.
Ensure data quality and security: AI-powered output can only be as good as the input, so it’s essential to ensure that data provided to AI systems is accurate, relevant and compliant with regulatory requirements. In addition, robust access controls and encryption mechanisms should be implemented to protect sensitive information and prevent unauthorized access.
Execute wisely: Start small and address a minimum-viable use case to demonstrate AI's value. Fail fast. Iterate based on user feedback and gradually expand implementation as appropriate. Ensure continuous monitoring of performance to drive ongoing improvement.
AI should be used to enhance productivity and the employee experience—not to replace employees. AI is like the ultimate assistant, being able to tackle complex tasks with ease and incredible speed, making it faster and easier for teams to do their jobs well. We’re still at the first few chapters of this emerging technology, but companies that stay at the forefront (cautiously and well-informed) will be positioned for ongoing advantage.

title: Council Post: Safeguarding Data Privacy In The Age Of AI Innovation
text:
Andres Zunino, ZirconTech cofounder and web development authority, drives innovation in Web3 for digital transformation.
As businesses rush to adopt generative artificial intelligence (AI) to fuel innovation and streamline operations, they can be met with significant privacy risks. This advanced technology, although promising, brings forth challenges for entities dealing with sensitive or proprietary data. The potential for data breaches and copyright conflicts is heightened when employing off-the-shelf AI solutions, highlighting the need for a careful approach to these technologies. It becomes essential for businesses to explore more secure, tailored AI solutions that provide control and help safeguard their critical information.
The Privacy Minefield Of Generative AI
Generative AI technologies have the beneficial ability to create a wide array of content, from textual to visual. However, this capability comes with significant privacy pitfalls that cannot be ignored. Utilizing generic AI platforms with proprietary data can lead to unintended disclosures and security breaches. There are documented cases in which sensitive training data was accidentally shared with unintended parties, eroding privacy and undermining competitive edges.
Moreover, copyright issues present a formidable hurdle. Generative AI inherently relies on extensive datasets for learning, which may include copyrighted materials. This involvement raises concerns over the authenticity and ownership of AI-generated outputs, further muddying the waters in an already complex legal domain for companies.
The OpenAI Paradigm: A Lesson In Flexibility And Uncertainty
The journey of OpenAI illustrates the fluid and unpredictable nature of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Originally founded as a nonprofit organization, OpenAI made the notable shift to a capped-profit entity, revealing the dynamic changes that can occur within AI companies' operational and financial frameworks. This transformation is not just a singular event but a broader indication of how AI enterprises may evolve, impacting their collaborations with other businesses.
For companies integrating third-party AI solutions into their operations, OpenAI's evolution underscores the reality that even pioneering AI organizations might alter their business models, including how they manage and utilize data. Such shifts could have profound implications for data privacy and ownership, especially for those entrusting their sensitive information to these platforms. It suggests that today's data management assurances might not be immutable, highlighting the importance of approaching third-party AI engagements with caution and an eye toward maintaining control over one's data.
Considering Custom AI Solutions For Enhanced Privacy And Control
Given the privacy challenges and risks associated with generic AI tools, the argument for custom, in-house AI solutions is stronger than ever. Developing personalized AI systems enables companies to hold complete ownership and command over their data, thereby reducing the likelihood of privacy breaches. These bespoke models, housed within an organization's own tech environment, are shielded from the unpredictability of external vendors' policies, and this can also reduce the risk of mishandling sensitive information.
Custom AI solutions are designed with the specific requirements of a business in mind, ensuring that the technology aligns with its unique goals and challenges. This tailored approach not only helps secure data more effectively but can also deliver a strategic advantage over competitors relying on standard AI offerings. Although investing in custom AI development demands a higher upfront cost, the payoff in terms of robust data protection, tailored operational efficiency and safeguarded intellectual property rights can justify the expenditure. Over time, these benefits contribute to a stronger, more secure foundation for leveraging AI technology without compromising the company's values or competitive position.
Exploring Alternatives For Secure AI Deployment
The Amazon Bedrock platform allows for the creation and deployment of machine learning models within a protected, scalable Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment. Amazon Bedrock enables companies to customize their AI applications for their specific business needs, allowing them to innovate without risking the privacy of their proprietary data.
In addition to Amazon Bedrock, several other self-hosting options provide the benefits of security and control. Companies can choose to set up their AI systems on private clouds or on-premises servers, depending on their specific requirements and preferences. This allows for a high degree of customization and helps ensure that sensitive information remains within the company's control, away from potential external threats.
For instance, Kubernetes is a powerful tool for orchestrating containerized AI applications, enhancing the manageability and efficiency of deploying AI solutions at scale. This open-source platform facilitates smooth operations and deployment processes, allowing businesses to focus on innovation while keeping their data secure.
Furthermore, cloud service providers like Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud offer specialized tools and services for building private AI environments. These platforms provide robust security features, extensive computational resources and flexible management options, making them suitable for businesses seeking to maintain a strong grip on their AI applications and data.
Securing The Future: Steering AI Innovation With Confidence
The journey from the vast capabilities of generative AI to the strategic shifts exemplified by OpenAI underscores the fluidity and uncertainty inherent in the AI landscape. This environment demands a vigilant approach toward data management, emphasizing the necessity for bespoke AI solutions that prioritize security and control.
The imperative for businesses to navigate the privacy challenges of AI with foresight and precision has never been more critical. Embracing custom, secure AI deployment models is not just a strategic advantage—it's a fundamental necessity for safeguarding the future of business innovation in the age of artificial intelligence.

title: AI For Justice: How A Female Founder Builds The Case For Lawyers
text:
Gila Hayat, cofounder and CTO of Darrow, is on a mission to use AI for good in the legal field. Her legal tech company's AI justice intelligence platform uses machine learning and natural language processing to identify potential cases, match law firms with the right expertise, and develop legal strategies in class action lawsuits.
Darrow is not only transforming the legal industry but also paving the way for more women in AI. While companies with female founders received 7.6% of global VC, an impressive 32.4% went to global VC in AI, according to PitchBook. Overall, this company's success highlights the potential of women's participation in AI and the importance of building successful, ethical, and impactful AI solutions.
Hayat and her team tackle lawyers' resistance to using AI by prioritizing accuracy and reliability, and building trust in Darrow’s AI tools.
Legal Tech Female Founder Develops AI For Good
Women's participation in founding AI companies and working in the industry is crucial for driving innovation, expanding the talent pool, promoting economic growth, ensuring ethical development, and using this powerful tool. Women represent only 22% of AI professionals globally, 14% of AI paper authors, and 18% of authors at the leading AI conferences. However, women are making greater strides as cofounders. Worldwide companies solely founded by women is 0.7%, mixed gender founding team is 31.7%. Nearly a third of companies (32.4%) of companies have women on the founding team, according to PitchBook.
Women’s diverse perspectives bring new ideas to the table and help identify and mitigate biases in AI systems. Women's participation in AI is a strategic imperative for building successful, ethical, and impactful AI solutions.
Hayat, cofounder and CTO at Darrow, is blazing the trail by using AI to help lawyers do more good. She was trained as a software developer in the Israeli army, especially AI. “[It] affected my views toward AI and how to use it for good,” she said
AI is revolutionizing fields such as law. With machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models working together, AI can automate tasks, improve legal research and analysis, and increase efficiency in the legal world to ensure justice prevails. It is transforming the way law is approached.
By analyzing news, social media, government filings, and consumer complaints, Darrow identifies wrongdoers so law firms can hold them accountable. The platform focuses on class-action lawsuits and forecasts their outcomes and value, then matches law firms with the right expertise to litigate. It connects the dots and finds patterns in case law.
Tasks like legal research are significantly streamlined with e-discovery, allowing lawyers to focus on strategy and client needs instead of tedious document reviews. Darrow is revolutionizing the detection of legal violations, shedding light on complex and subtle breaches previously undetected.
With AI as a powerful ally, lawyers can reveal violations in a wide range of areas, such as:
- Finance: Securities fraud, deceptive marketing practices.
- Consumer Protection: Defective products, data breaches.
- Employment: Wage theft, discrimination.
- Healthcare: Defective medical devices, pharmaceutical wrongdoings.
- Environment: Environmental pollution violations.
The boom in AI has accelerated the company’s trajectory. It launched in 2020 and was accepted into Y Combinator in the winter of 2021. “It was a great experience for us,” said Hayat. Y Combinator provides seed funding, mentorship, access to funders, validation, and accountability.
"It’s rare to find a team with both the deep legal and tech backgrounds needed to pull this off — Elad [Spiegelman, cofounder] and Evya [Ben Artzi, cofounder] clerked in the Israeli Supreme Court and Gila had a background as a software developer and data scientist solving complex intelligence related problems," said Aaron Epstein, group partner of Y Combinator. The company has a team of nearly 100 with many legal experts and technologists, and has raised $59 million.
For Hayat, developing software is akin to creating art, as both involve creativity, expression, aesthetics, craftsmanship, and problem-solving. The iterative process, collaboration, interdisciplinary work, and cultural influence also play a significant role in developing successful products. Viewing software development as an art form highlights its human-centric nature and the importance of innovation and impact in creating products that enrich users' lives.
Winning Trust And Confidence: Tackling AI Challenges Among Lawyers
The legal profession embraces legal tech in some areas, from e-discovery and contract management to client communication and data security. Still, there are concerns about incorporating newer technologies such as AI. Concerns include accuracy and reliability, security, learning curves, and cultural resistance. It’s Hayat who ensures that the platform addresses these concerns.
“The biggest challenge in AI today is understanding how deep [legal] professionals think,” Hayat said. “The legal profession requires years of knowledge but also a lot of intuition.” Her goal is to translate the way people think and communicate into a technology language model that is applied to the legal system.
“We fine-tune our language models with legal information, ensuring our decisions are accurate and trustworthy,” said Hayat. “This is especially important in legal decision-making and assessing facts, where we must carefully verify sources and understand their truth. Our systems are designed to align with a story's legal standpoint and factual background, providing a strong foundation of trust for our clients.” Because laws differ from country to country, Darrow is currently focused on the U.S.
“Clients trust us because our AI tools provide accurate results that can't be achieved elsewhere,” said Hayat. “Darrow has been a great tech partner for the firm,” said Lewis Kahn, founding partner of Kahn Swick & Foti. “Their team is hands on and the best we’ve seen in 30 years of my practice.” “Darrow has been a great partner for us.,” said Jon Loevy, founding partner of Loevy & Loevy. “Their team is unbelievably smart, doing cutting edge data projects.”
The legal profession is just beginning to learn how to harness the power of language models by shifting their mindset from writing queries to asking good questions, a skill that lawyers excel at. “It's more like you're interviewing Darrow,” said Hayat. “You get a good answer because you asked a really good question.”
The company is obsessed with improving its clients' outcomes. It does this by continually validating and improving the platform's performance.

title: 3 AI Stocks Everyone’s Missed
text:
AI stocks are booming—but they’re an absolute “dividend desert” for us contrarian income-seekers.
Or are they?
Most tech stocks—and I’d put AI darling NVIDIA (NVDA), with its pathetic 0.02% yield, at the top of the list here—don’t pay dividends when they’re growing quickly.
Only later, when growth slows, do they “find religion” and return cash to shareholders as dividends and buybacks. That’s too bad for those of us who like to have more than one way—price gains—to book returns on our stocks.
But what if we could find a way to grab more of our AI profits as dividends—particularly growing dividends—so we don’t have to “buy and hope” for price gains alone?
We can if we employ a “pick and shovel” approach.
During the gold rush of the 1840s, hordes flocked to California to get rich mining for gold. But the guys who made the real money didn’t actually mine anything. They were the entrepreneurs who sold the “pick and shovels” (as well as booze and lodging) to the hapless speculators.
3 “Pick-and-Shovel” Dividends to Cash in on the AI “Gold Rush”
The three stocks we’ll talk about next are ideal “pick and shovel” plays on the AI boom: The first is a California- (and Texas-) based utility set to profit as AI drives power demand through the roof—to 85 terawatts a year by 2027, according to Scientific American. That’s more power than many small countries use.
Another is an apartment landlord whose ultra-modern units are coveted by Silicon Valley’s tech set. This “back-door” play on tech’s—and AI’s—ongoing growth has hiked payouts for 30 straight years. The third is a cell-tower operator that’ll benefit as AI-powered apps drive up data demand.
Let’s get going, starting with …
Sempra: AI’s Heavy-Duty “Battery”
Sempra (SRE) is the utility that’s best-positioned to leverage AI’s bottomless appetite for electricity, thanks to its presence in two of America’s top tech markets—one well-established (California), and one many folks see as the next Silicon Valley: Texas.
Let’s start with California, where Sempra has 25 million customers in the southern and central parts of the state. Despite recent tech layoffs (more on those below), California created 260,000 jobs in 2023, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, a rate that matched pre-pandemic levels.
But Texas, where Sempra has 13 million customers and operates 143,000 miles of transmission lines, is the real growth driver here.
The state’s tech sector is en fuego: according to the Texas Economic Development Corporation, 17,600 tech firms now call Texas home, where they employ some 203,700 workers. In Austin alone, the number of tech jobs jumped 9.8% in 2022, according to the city’s chamber of commerce.
All of this builds a strong case for Sempra—and its stellar earnings history drives the point home—management continuously sets a 6% to 8% EPS-growth target … and continuously crushes it!
No wonder the payout (current yield: 3.5%) is on a growth tear .. and it’s pulled up the share price with it, too. That connection is a phenomenon I call the “Dividend Magnet”—and we’ve seen in dividend stock after dividend stock. Watch it work its magic:
Check out that orange line, which pops every time Sempra hikes its payout. Until recently, that is, when the rate panic hit the stock (just as it did with pretty well all bonds and “bond proxies” like utilities). That’s our opportunity to pounce, before Sempra’s price (inevitably) closes the gap with the payout.
Essex Property Trust: Reliable Payouts From the “Home” of AI
Our next “hidden” AI dividend is a real estate investment trust (REIT) with thousands of apartments in Silicon Valley.
That might sound like a bit of a strange move, given the tech-sector layoffs we’ve seen. But panics like these are exactly when we contrarians unearth our best dividend deals. And in this case, the layoffs the media breathlessly rambles on about are really just a correction after Meta Platforms (META) and friends overdid it in the pandemic.
Here are the facts: even with the layoffs, the 20 biggest tech firms still employ 37,000 more people than they did in 2019, according to the Silicon Valley Index. And growth is returning, with the area adding 2,700 net jobs from June 2022 to June 2023.
And now, with the AI arms race running hot—with $17.9 billion going into AI start-ups alone in the third quarter of 2023—and other tech trends (remember cloud computing?) still going strong, now is a good time to invest in the region at a bargain.
Essex Property Trust (ESS) is a great way to do it. The REIT pays 3.8% and has 62,000 units across three tech hotspots: northern California, southern California and Seattle, with the bulk of its net operating income coming from the former two—exactly the setup we want for our AI-powered real estate dividend!
Heck, there’s even an EV angle here, with Essex having a presence in Fremont, California, home to a Tesla (TSLA) Gigafactory!
These forces are all supporting Essex’s cash flow—and dividend, which has grown yearly for 30 straight years.
Dividend magnet? Check! Essex’s share price has tracked its payout point for point. And as with Sempra, we’re getting that same buy window, as the price has (for now) fallen behind the payout, mainly due to overwrought worries that rates will stay high:
The dividend is safe, with occupancy at 96.3% (measured on a preliminary basis for January and February 2024), delinquencies at 1.5% (down 40 basis points from the 2023 average) and same-property revenue forecast to rise 1.7% in 2024. A more sustainable hiring pace in Silicon Valley will drive that growth going forward.
SBA Communications: AI’s “Wiring”
Finally, let’s round out our AI-powered portfolio with SBA Communications (SBAC), which has 40,000 towers in North America, South America and Africa.
AI-powered apps will only make cellphones more addictive (yep, it’s possible!). Not good news for conversation, but great news for SBA. The company only began paying a dividend in 2019. And the payout has been on a growth tear since, surging 130%.
The stock was on a tear, too. But then 2022 hit, rates rose, and SBA sank with other REITs. Management kept paying its dividend, raising it annually, but it didn’t matter. The rate freight train temporarily flattened SBA shares:
Cell towers are a costly business to build but a fantastic one to run. It’s expensive to erect a tower, but the wily operator can then add a second and third tenant to the tower at a minimal incremental cost.
SBA’s dividend reflects this, but its stock price does not. Thank you, higher rates, for giving us a rare opportunity to buy this company in the bargain bin.
Vanilla investors see SBA’s 1.8% yield and yawn, but we contrarians know better. But unlike with, say, NVIDIA, which can only pay us through price gains, we have three ways to win with SBA:
The 1.8% yield.
- The potential for the stock to surge when rates fall. After all, SBA’s price must catch up with its Dividend Magnet.
- Future dividend increases, to the tune of 20%+ yearly if history is any guide.
Finally, we’re nicely set up geographically here. While SBA’s main competitors, American Tower (AMT) and Crown Castle International (CCI), have expanded across the globe, SBAC does three-quarters of its business in the US.
That’s exactly where we want to be as American growth rolls on, thanks in part to megatrends like AI-driven productivity gains and the continued “onshoring” of manufacturing as more US companies move their operations home.

title: Power To The People: Putting AI To Work With RapidCanvas
text:
For Rahul Pangam, CEO of RapidCanvas, the journey to the artificial intelligence (AI) platform he co-founded in 2023, began more than 15 years ago. “I was working at Google, and I was asked to support the growing number of fraud experts it was hiring because they didn’t know how to code,” he recalls. “I had to find a way for them to put their expertise to work without having to train as software engineers.”
Texas-based RapidCanvas, which is today announcing the successful completion of a $7.5 million funding round, is Pangam’s latest effort to rise to that challenge. “What I realised in that role at Google is that the people in a business who know how to do the technical tasks are not necessarily the people who understand the business problem that actually needs solving,” he says. “We need to empower those problem solvers to take the lead.”
RapidCanvas’s value proposition is based on that proposition. AI and machine learning (ML) technologies offer huge opportunities for businesses to operate more effectively and efficiently – and to do so across multiple functions. The RapidCanvas platform therefore aims to help people throughout the business to put such technology to work in their specific areas of responsibility, even if they know nothing at all about how to build and use AI and ML tools.
Pangam co-founded the business with Uttam Phalnikar, with whom he previously launched Simility an ML-based risk management platform that was eventually acquired by PayPal. The duo saw an opportunity to build on their previous experience amid the emergence of large language models (LLMs) and generative AI (GenAI).
Indeed, Pangam argues that GenAI is the obvious answer to the age-old problem of business experts not knowing how to build technical solutions. “If you ask it the right questions, GenAI will generate the code you need for a given problem,” he points out. “That is transformational for people like me who have been thinking about this mismatch for the past 15 years.”
Based on such developments, RapidCanvas’s platform offers businesses a three-stage process to building AI models for their most urgent problems – and is aimed at business users who may have no technical knowledge of AI and ML at all.
The first stage, leveraging GenAI, is for the user to tell the platform what data they currently have and what problem they are seeking to solve. It will then make suggestions for what additional data might be required, as well as identifying any problems with the existing data.
Next, once the dataset is finalised, the platform uses an autonomous AI-building technology to construct the model – Pangam says RapidCanvas can do this work in a few minutes, where even a professional data scientist might take several weeks. The model can then be tested and iterated over and again to improve it.
Finally, the platform provides a read-out of how the model arrives at its conclusions. “It gives you the detail of what lies behind its scores and predictions,” explains Pangam. “That’s important because CEOs will naturally be sceptical – they need to be able to understand why the model is telling them what it is.”
In theory, this process could be applied to almost any business problem, but RapidCanvas has focused on around 50 common issues where AI is often seen as most potentially valuable. It has developed libraries of solutions that users can adopt, split into business problems spanning risk management, marketing, logistics and manufacturing, predictive maintenance, and sales.
So far, the company has attracted around 25 customers from a range of different industries. One early adopter, automotive parts manufacture MTE-THOMSON, cites the role played by the platform in significant business gains.
“Our vision was to integrate AI into our demand prediction and inventory management processes,” explains Arthur Strommer, a vice president at MTE-THOMSON. “We've seen a 35% improvement in operational efﬁciency and a 50% reduction in time spent on manual adjustments, eliminating operational bottlenecks and streamlining our processes.”
That sort of testimonial has impressed potential investors in the business, with today’s $7.5 million round led by Accel, with participation from Valley Capital Partners.
“While the potential of AI has become increasingly obvious to enterprises around the world, their ability to incorporate AI solutions into their operations is limited by time, talent, and money,” says Dinesh Katiyar, a partner at Accel. “RapidCanvas has created a unique solution to this problem, providing business users with a co-pilot that enables them to build AI solutions speciﬁc to their needs, quickly and economically.”
The seed funding is earmarked for investment in further product development, as well as in the sales and marketing function. For Pangam, however, this already feels like coming full circle from his days at Google. “So many people are excited by the potential of AI but unsure how to exploit it,” he says. “It’s really rewarding to be able to empower them.”

title: Council Post: How To Harmonize AI And Data Integration For Seamless Innovation
text:
Director of Data Integration Specialist at CEPTUA IT INC.
AI and data integration are no longer siloed entities; they are dynamic forces converging to reshape industries. AI, with its ability to analyze vast datasets and derive actionable insights, can greatly increase a company's informed decision-making. Simultaneously, data integration can facilitate the aggregation of diverse data sources, breaking down informational barriers within organizations.
In the rapidly evolving realm of technology, the union of artificial intelligence (AI) and data integration has been driving innovation. I've seen the importance of harmonizing horizons in AI and data integration in my experience in the tech industry and have recognized how leveraging this synergy can propel innovation in your business. Let's dive in.
The Fusion Of Forces
Fusing the forces of AI and data integration is akin to orchestrating a symphony, where each instrument (AI and data integration) plays a complementary role in achieving harmony. Rather than viewing them as separate initiatives, I recommend aiming for an integrated approach that envisions AI as a natural extension of data integration.
Navigating The Landscape And Harmonizing Horizons
The landscapes of AI and data integration are diverse. Navigating this terrain requires a strategic approach that considers the company's unique needs and goals.
To begin, evaluate your existing infrastructure. Start by conducting an audit of the data ecosystem to identify all data sources and assess their quality, accessibility and compatibility. Determine how data flows within your organization and where bottlenecks or inefficiencies exist. Additionally, analyze the current analytics capabilities and identify areas where AI could enhance insights and decision-making processes. This evaluation should provide a comprehensive understanding of your company's data landscape and highlight areas ripe for AI integration.
Harmonizing horizons, in the context of AI and data integration, means aligning the goals and functionalities of these technologies to work seamlessly together. Here are a few ways you can create a synergy where the capabilities of AI and data integration complement and enhance each other.
1. Break Down Silos
One of the primary challenges businesses face is the existence of data silos, where information is confined to specific departments or systems. To break down data silos, identify them, promote sharing, form cross-functional teams, standardize data formats and invest in integration technologies. In my experience, steps like these help foster collaboration and ensure AI insights stem from a comprehensive dataset, leading to more accurate outcomes.
2. Invest In Continuous Learning And Adaptation
Invest in AI capabilities that support adaptive algorithms. This fosters continuous learning and adaptation. Implement feedback loops for monitoring performance and data quality management. Encourage your leadership and team members to experiment, collaborate and stay updated on industry trends.
3. Support Scalability And Flexibility
Foster flexibility and scalability by enabling modular architecture, cloud-based solutions, containerization, API-driven integration, automated provisioning, scalable data storage and performance monitoring. These approaches help ensure that AI and data integration systems can evolve with business growth, staying aligned with your organizational needs.
4. Leverage Enhanced Customer Experiences
AI-driven insights, derived from integrated data sources, have the potential to enable more personalized and targeted approaches that enhance the overall customer experience. Ways to do this include utilizing customer relationship management (CRM) platforms, sentiment analysis tools and customer journey mapping techniques. Reputable resources like Gartner or Forrester reports can also provide insights into best practices for enhancing customer experiences through AI and data integration.
5. Optimize Your Operations
Integrated AI and data integration can help optimize operational processes. Predictive analytics can foresee bottlenecks, streamline workflows and boost efficiency. To learn more, refer to reputable sources like McKinsey's report on AI in operations. To achieve optimized operations, ensure data quality by leveraging advanced analytics tools and fostering a data-driven culture. Training employees and regularly assessing performance during the integration process can also help you achieve the best results.
6. Visualize Data For More Informed Decision-Making
The synergy of AI and data integration can allow you to make more informed decisions and strategic choices for the business by granting access to comprehensive, real-time data. Data quality is once again important to getting the most from these insights. Visualization techniques can be effective tools for facilitating clearer understanding between teams. Case studies from Deloitte or Harvard Business Review showcase other ways to make effective decision-making through AI and data integration.
Overcoming Challenges On The Horizon
While the concept of harmonizing horizons has great potential, it is not without its challenges. Businesses must navigate issues such as data security, ethical AI use and the need for more skilled personnel. Additionally, integrating AI and data integration requires a thoughtful approach to ensure compatibility and avoid disruptions.
Some of the ways you can address these challenges include a commitment to transparency, robust cybersecurity measures and ongoing training programs. Foster a culture of responsibility within your workplace to help ensure that the benefits of harmonizing horizons are realized without compromising your organization's ethical standards or data integrity.
Conclusion
Harmonizing horizons in the realm of AI and data integration is a holistic approach that, when done effectively, can transform a business into an agile, innovative entity. By breaking down silos, fostering continuous learning and embracing scalability, you can navigate the landscape of technology with confidence.

title: Council Post: Join The AI Revolution: Transforming Patient Care At Your Fingertips
text:
Erez Meltzer, CEO & Board Member of Nanox, is a prominent Israel business leader with 35+ years experience leading various global companies.
In 2015, world leaders committed to providing health services for all people by 2030. However, as the World Health Organization (WHO) reported in 2023, we're only halfway toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) target of achieving universal health coverage by 2030. Progress is slow, and the field of healthcare is presented with the challenge of not only continuing to innovate disease therapies, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, treatment machinery and other cutting-edge medicines but also finding a way to share these developments with people across the world, of all socioeconomic statuses.
Geographic, infrastructural and socioeconomic divides highlight stark disparities in healthcare access. As we strive for global health equity, innovation, particularly in medical technology, therapeutics and AI, becomes paramount. Inequities in healthcare access directly impact patient outcomes. Early detection, precise diagnoses, effective treatments and ongoing medical monitoring can be life-changing. Yet, many communities worldwide lack these essential healthcare resources. To bridge this gap, we must strengthen networks of healthcare professionals, payers and companies, ensuring access to valuable treatments and tools globally.
For instance, AI offers the potential to enable physicians to interpret radiology images without requiring specialized expertise. AI-powered clinical decision support tools are paving the way for doctors to provide accurate interpretations quickly, even in regions where access to specialized radiologists is limited. This widening access to expertise has the potential to significantly transform healthcare delivery globally, especially in underserved regions.
To achieve equitable healthcare outcomes, we must prioritize global healthcare investments. This necessitates increased government funding and public spending on healthcare infrastructure, bolstering both domestic and international programs. Tackling global health disparities requires a collective effort, recognizing that no single country can accomplish this monumental task alone. Funding should primarily support primary healthcare initiatives, such as local clinics staffed with health professionals capable of delivering about 90% of essential health services, as reported by the WHO.
Investment in global health benefits not only struggling regions but also stimulates widespread economic growth and social development. According to the WHO, "While public spending remains the primary source of health funding, countries struggle to find the funds needed for universal health coverage. Simultaneously, the world economy and national budgets are under strain. Development assistance faces constraints. Health services require new funding sources and innovative products to leverage private sector resources." This underscores the global appetite for innovation, extending healthcare advancements to all corners of the world.
Technology Progresses While Healthcare Lags Behind
Another point to consider is that the United States, despite its considerable resources, has yet to fully harness the potential of AI innovation and technology to restore its antiquated healthcare system, which currently lags behind. While the nation possesses the means to drive AI advancements, there is room for improvement in integrating these technologies into healthcare systems effectively.
In recent years, the U.S. has made substantial strides in AI research and development. However, these advancements have not been seamlessly integrated into the nation's healthcare infrastructure. Despite having access to cutting-edge technology and an abundance of healthcare data, the implementation of AI-driven solutions in clinical practice remains somewhat fragmented. The healthcare system continues to grapple with interoperability challenges, data privacy concerns and the need for standardized protocols. To fully realize AI's potential, the nation must take a comprehensive approach, addressing not only technological innovation but also the necessary regulatory frameworks and workforce training.
Additionally, while AI has the potential to enhance healthcare accessibility and quality across the board, the U.S. and global healthcare systems have faced hurdles in ensuring equitable distribution of AI-enabled tools and services. Disparities in access to care persist, with marginalized communities often having limited access to the benefits of AI-driven healthcare.
Recent examples of healthcare companies focusing on equity-driven initiatives highlight the transformative power of technology. Pfizer's four-year partnership with Zipline harnesses drone technology to enhance global access to care. Zipline's drones deliver vital supplies like blood, vaccines and essential medicines, showcasing modern technology's potential in global healthcare delivery. This initiative targets "last mile" communities in resource-limited rural areas, aiming to close health equity gaps. Similarly, the WHO's Be He@lthy, Be Mobile (BHBM) initiative, which has been ongoing since 2012, has already reached millions worldwide. BHBM collaborates with governments to scale up targeted client communication messaging services for noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and their risk factors. This initiative illustrates the positive impact of mobile and wireless technologies, paving the way for accessibility to essential early detection tools, such as medical imaging for diagnoses and treatment.
Addressing global healthcare equity gaps may appear daunting, but practical approaches offer tangible progress. Technology, innovation and partnerships are pivotal in enhancing healthcare access. Numerous initiatives, like the Johns Hopkins Innovation + Design Enabling Access (IDEA) Initiative, are already underway. These efforts focus on expanding healthcare infrastructure, deploying new technologies and building workforces in underserved regions. Collaborative endeavors among stakeholders, including governments, regions and innovative companies, are essential for driving sustained progress toward global healthcare equity.
AI To Help Everyone—Not Just Those At The Top
The quest for global health equity remains a pressing challenge. While the world grapples with disparities in healthcare access, technological innovations, partnerships and increased investment hold the promise of bringing transformative change. The potential for AI to bridge gaps in healthcare, empower physicians and improve outcomes is substantial. To achieve universal health coverage by 2030, nations, organizations and innovators must continue their collaborative efforts to ensure healthcare becomes accessible to all, regardless of geographic or socioeconomic constraints.

title: Council Post: The Emerging LLM Stack In Investment Funds
text:
Moyi Dang, Cofounder and Data Scientist at Coinfeeds. Writes about the emerging LLM stack at Mati Labs.
As a data scientist, I have been working with language model technologies since 2019. In 2021, I founded Coinfeeds, a company that collaborates with investment funds to provide data science and AI solutions. In this role, I have had numerous discussions with technology leaders at these funds, gaining insights into how they leverage and implement AI.
What I've learned is that ChatGPT can increase productivity in the workplace, assisting with writing emails, summarizing research papers and writing code and documentation. Portfolio managers and analysts, in particular, see significant productivity enhancements when AI can interact with internal research reports and meeting notes. These use cases, when set up properly, can significantly boost a firm's overall efficiency.
Adoption still faces barriers and risks, and investment firms can gain the most benefits and can be unlocked when AI can access internal documents. That said, a large language model (LLM) stack is emerging to accommodate new use cases and address concerns.
Foundation For AI Success
Before examining why to build an LLM stack and the emerging strategies for managing it, let's look at some of the key factors that determine success:
Data Foundations
A successful AI strategy lies on top of solid data foundations. This can require transitioning from legacy technology infrastructures developed over decades to modern data warehousing. This is because pre-trained AI models still need integration with internal data sources to be useful for real business applications.
Legacy systems often have data trapped in silos, stored in incompatible formats and are difficult to access and analyze holistically. With modern data warehousing solutions, companies can bring together data from heterogeneous sources, enforce common data standards and create an integrated data platform. This provides a unified view of data for AI algorithms to work with.
Technical Talent
Implementing AI in investment funds is strongly linked to the scale of their technical teams. Engineers, quantitative analysts and data scientists typically spearhead the adoption of AI, identifying innovative applications for the broader organization.
When developing or implementing new AI products, it will be important for these teams to collaborate with other stakeholders to discover unique uses—such as news summary alerts and automated invoice processing—that serve internal product managers.
Leadership Support
AI adoption is a complex process that requires strong leadership support. For investment firms to see success with AI adoption, they must first manage diverse stakeholder interests and collect potential applications from internal users.
Likewise, it is important to assess a range of technologies and orchestrate pilot projects while listening to and addressing concerns raised by legal, risk and compliance teams.
Key Considerations For AI
As organizations explore the adoption of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, there are several key considerations to keep in mind regarding their limitations, optimization approaches and provider choices. This section outlines some of the critical factors companies should evaluate when leveraging LLMs.
Current Limitations Of LLMs
Some professionals have expressed disappointment with the recent hype surrounding LLMs. Quantitative researchers have utilized advanced machine learning and data mining for decades, and they are often the most skeptical of chatbots like ChatGPT. Quants find that ChatGPT is not great at mathematical reasoning, which is crucial for bond valuation, option pricing and risk management tasks.
When it comes to ChatGPT and coding, some programmers find it more effective than others. Also, concerns arise over the risk of errors from unverified machine-generated code and ChatGPT's limited ability to refactor large legacy codebases.
RAG Vs. Finetuning
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and finetuning are methods to improve language models. RAG integrates external information during generation while finetuning trains a model to a specific dataset for enhanced task performance.
In finance, RAG may be preferable for its immediate benefits, as finetuning might be unnecessary unless dealing with entirely new data. Given RAG's efficiency, it is likely the more appealing option.
OpenAI vs Open Source
Sophisticated investment managers can explore open-source and alternative LLM providers, carefully considering their choices compared to OpenAI. It's important to conduct experiments where internal users can choose between multiple LLMs.
These experiments can be set up as blind A/B tests, where internal users can ask the same question to two or more different models, and select which response they prefer. Examples of this model can be found online, such as the LMSYS chatbot arena.
The LLM stack
Once your team has an understanding of the concepts and considerations, it's time to start building the stack:
The Basic LLM Tech Stack
The basic LLM setup features an internal ChatGPT-like system with data and IP protection, including a user interface for document uploads.
It's important to establish a guardrail layer to ensure confidentiality and proper use, along with logging for compliance. Using OpenAI services in an Azure VPC is one way to keep data secure, as Microsoft says it will not use customer data for training.
Connecting LLMs to Internal Data Sources
For investment funds, the true potential of LLMs is unlocked through their integration with internal data sources. This process entails converting unstructured data, like Word documents and PDF files, into a format suitable for a vector database.
LLMs then interact with these vector databases using RAG. While conceptually straightforward, building a robust infrastructure to support this can be challenging.
The ideal setup provides the LLM seamless access to diverse, interconnected datasets. However, data is often fragmented across legacy systems that don't easily link together. Assembling a useful knowledge base from disparate sources requires overcoming considerable technical hurdles. The payoff for solving these systems integration problems is more capable, intelligently informed LLMs.
Application Development
It's important to go beyond merely integrating existing AI tools but to also actively develop downstream applications. These applications are tailored for particular workflows, such as completing forms or executing specific tasks to streamline the investment process.
Conclusion
AI undoubtedly has the potential to enhance productivity within organizations significantly. However, it's crucial to remain aware of its limitations and associated risks. Data foundation and investment in technical talent will be vital in getting organizations ready for AI.

title: Cerebras Partners With Qualcomm, Launches 3rd-Gen Wafer-Scale AI
text:
The newest system from Cerebras can handle multi-trillion parameter generative AI problems at twice the performance of its predecessor, while partnering with Qualcomm will help them cut inference processing costs by 10X.
Cerebras Systems, the innovative startup who’s wafer-scale AI engines have garnered significant customer following and hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, has launched its latest salvo in the war with Nvidia and anyone else who stands in their way. The new CS3 system, the third in the industry’s only commercial wafer-scale AI processor, is built on TSMC 5nm process and is immediately available. The company is also partering with Qualcomm, optimizing the output from the CS3 to cut inference costs with co-developed technology.
Its not really fair to compare a complete wafer of chips to a single Nvidia GPU, but if you do, you immediately see the advantage of not slicing the wafer into individual chips which are then reconnected via CPUs and networking. The compute and memory density is off the charts, with 900,000 AI cores and 44 GB of fast (~10X HBM) on-wafer memory. Additional memory for large AI problems is supplied in a separate MemoryX parameter server.
The four trillion transistors on a WSE-3 interconnect across the wafer, dramatically speeding processing times for generative AI. And the Cerebras software stack enables AI problems to scale efficiently across a CS3 cluster (the complete system housing a wafer) at a fraction of the development effort needed to distribute a problem across a cluster of accelerators. A faster chip, a faster cluster, and much faster time to deploy AI has helped Cerebras earn the support of organizations like the Mayo Clinic and Glaxo-Smith Klein.
Big AI needs big memory. In a GPU-based cluster, that means using expensive High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) modules and 3D chip stacking, which slows down and complicates the supply chain. In a Cerebras CS3 cluster, it means complementing the faster on-wafer SRAM with a memory server called the MemoryX. which serves up parameters from a 2.4 Petabyte appliance. The result is faster and larger AI in a single rack vs. a cluster of over 10,000 GPUs or Google TPUs.
Cerebras has been collaborating with UAE-based G42 to build a distributed network of what will soon be nine data centers full of Cerebras tech. The next data center of the constellation, the Condor Galaxy 3, is already being built in Dallas using the new CS-3 servers. The two companies are on track to complete all nine of the Galaxy supercomputers by the end of this year, creating a massive AI system for internal G42 use and to provide cloud services.
Collaboration with Qualcomm
One of the advantages that Nvidia has enjoyed is inference-aware training and post-processing, where the output of the training run is optimized to run faster on a specific inference processor (GPU). Since Qualcomm is rapidly becoming the industry leader in edge AI, they needed to partner with someone (other than Nvidia) to realize the potential benefits of working with a training platform company.
The Wafer-scale Engine offers a unique alternative to Nvidia, AMD, Intel, and Google. But it isn’t ideal for large-throughput inference processing serving thousands of simultaneous users. Instead of telling its customers to go pick a GPU, Cerebras has decided to collaborate with Qualcomm, which has turned its Snapdragon AI engine into an inference appliance, the Cloud AI100, which beats all other vendors in the MLPerf benchmark tests in energy efficiency.
Qualcomm AI Research has been developing a variety of techniques to fit large AI models onto mobile Snapdragon chips. This research enabled Cerebras to apply three initial approaches to optimize AI models for inference processing on its Cloud AI100 Ultra, a platform that has garnered support from a lengthy list of partners, most recently AWS and HPE. The two companies have applied sparsity, speculative decoding, and MX6 compression to the training stack on the CS3. By using these techniques, Cerebras is able to provide inference-target-aware output of the training process, lowering the cost of inference by 10X.
We have always thought that the industry needs to cut inference costs by two orders of magnitude by the end of this decade. Now, 10X has already been achieved, so I think we underestimated the pace of innovation.
By teaming together, Cerebras and Qualcomm can now provide an end-to-end high performance AI platform, from training to inference processing. Without Qualcomm, Cerebras would have had to partner with Nvidia to achieve similar results, an unlikely pairing to say the least. Now they can address customers’ entire AI workflow with an optimized solution.
Conclusions
As AI moves from research to invaluable tool, and from the cloud to the edge, the end-t0-end workflow needs to be thought about holistically to produce business value. These two companies have demonstrated both a remarkable grasp of AI fundamentals and the ability to execute reliably.

title: Gen AI Is Rising Fast: How We Ensure Black Americans Rise With It
text:
Since generative artificial intelligence (gen AI) burst on the scene in late 2022, businesses, governments, and individuals have been trying to figure out not only what it can do, but whether it would be a net positive. In 2023, McKinsey estimated that gen AI could add the equivalent of $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion a year to the global economy by 2040. For the United States, which dominates gen AI investment, it could boost labor productivity and economic growth.
But history shows that big changes are never that straightforward. What may look like an economic boon overall can mean pain to some individuals or groups. For example, the report notes that two-thirds of US jobs are exposed to AI-driven automation; a quarter of current tasks could be automated right now. Some degree of disruption and displacement is inevitable.
With that in mind, it’s worth asking: What are the implications of gen AI for Black Americans specifically? The answer is: it depends.
For example, take household wealth. Gen AI could add almost $500 billion, or $3,400 per US household, by 2045. But that average figure hides the very unequal distribution of wealth. The median Black household has one-eighth the wealth of the median white. Unless these underlying patterns change substantially, and more Black-owned businesses engage in the gen AI space, receiving the fair share of venture capital funding, the rise of gen AI could exacerbate the racial wealth gap.
Or consider workforce dynamics. Black Americans are overrepresented in four sectors—office support, factory work, food services, and mechanical installation and repair—that are likely to see a great deal of automation. The concern is that such changes could mean job losses—and Black Americans already have higher than average unemployment (5.2%, compared to 3.7% for the US population as a whole). These trends pre-date gen AI, and in fact, one of the characteristics of gen AI is the way it could impact higher-skilled work, such as pharmaceutical research, legal services, and investment banking.
Specifically, it could greatly affect the middle tier of the workforce—high-mobility jobs that pay at least $42,000, that offer significant career progression, and that don’t require a college degree. In the past five years, one in eight Black Americans have moved into this kind of work, which provides a ladder to economic mobility. Over time, however, gen AI could perform all or most of these jobs, in effect cutting out several rungs. For example, intensive coding programs such as boot camps have opened well-paid tech work to those without college degrees, but these are exactly the kinds of entry-level jobs that gen AI is well equipped to do.
On the positive side, the effective use of gen AI could also benefit Black Americans in important ways. For example, there are already cases where AI has been used to improve care for pregnant women, reducing maternal mortality and the incidence of pre-term births—both of which are much more prevalent among Black Americans. Gen AI could help healthcare providers build on such initiatives, for example, by drafting care plans in plain language, synthesizing patient histories, reminding patients of what they need to do, and providing an easily accessible first point of contact. In education, it could expand opportunities by making high-quality personalized tutors more accessible to all learners. Gen AI could also help to close the financial inclusion gap. It’s worth noting that many Black Americans are comfortable with non-traditional banking. Roughly 14% of Black adults have a digital bank as their primary provider, compared to 8% of white adults, and are also more likely to use digital payment services. Gen AI could help Black banking consumers in several ways, including financial planning, equitable access to credit, and personalized product offerings.
So, it’s a mixed bag. If gen AI is to develop in a way that benefits all Americans, that needs to be done intentionally: it won’t just happen. For one thing, gen AI is only as good (or not so good) as the underlying data and algorithms. To the extent that these contain biases, the outcomes will be flawed.
For another, while it is not clear exactly how gen AI will affect the workforce, it is certain that it will. Companies should be thinking now about how to re-skill workers at risk of gen AI displacement. No job is future-proof; the emphasis, for both workers and employers, should be on honing future-proof skills.
Gen AI is still new; developing equitable strategies and applications from the start makes sense. If this transition is managed well, gen AI can play a role in promoting a fairer, more inclusive economy.

title: Council Post: 2024 Trends Driving Strategic Shifts In Customer Support Strategies
text:
Sagar Rajgopal is the president and chief customer officer (CCO) of Ubiquity, a leading outsourcer for disruptive brands.
As the complexity of doing business around the globe increases and businesses prioritize a sharp focus on what they know, I anticipate that one of 2024’s biggest overall trends will be a surge in outsourcing processes.
Businesses can’t and shouldn’t be experts in all aspects of their business. As chief customer officer of a leading outsourcer, I can confirm from personal experience that outsourcing tasks or processes that are outside of an organization’s operational wheelhouse can boost efficiency, streamline workflows, give businesses access to the latest expertise and technology and potentially help lower costs and drive sales.
With customer experience (CX) being such a vital piece for business success, it is often one of the first processes to get outsourced. CX professionals will have plenty to juggle in 2024 with new technologies, risks and shifting customer expectations shaking things up.
Among the many developments driving an overall increase in outsourcing, these are the most important trends creating strategic shifts in CX this year.
Navigating The Future With AI
It would be a massive understatement to say that generative AI was 2023’s biggest disruptor, especially when it comes to CX. This year, changes to the industry brought on by AI will continue to make waves (and likely will for years to come). While the rise of AI, natural language processing (NLP) and advanced analytics offer many benefits, including the promise of efficiency, a cautionary trend emerges—organizations risking consumer skepticism and distrust of AI. A recent study by Redpoint Global found that 77% of consumers believe positive customer experiences still need an element of human touch.
In the year ahead, customer service will benefit from an increased focus on the delicate balance needed between new technology, such as AI, and the benefits of human support engagement.
In my opinion, AI should be viewed as an augmentation of human capabilities. In certain interactions, human empathy and problem-solving skills remain irreplaceable. For every element of added value AI brings, a human needs to be working in the background to help set up learning (data collection, annotation and evaluation), guard rails and audits. This will be especially vital as governments look to put more AI-related controls in place, particularly in regulated industries.
In the pursuit of efficiency gains, organizations must tread carefully to avoid overlooking the value of human interaction in customer support.
Increasing Regulatory Complexity
The 2023 Global Business Complexity Index found that the global regulatory burden is expected to increase. When it comes to CX, for American organizations, I believe one of the biggest impacts from regulatory updates will likely stem from restrictions around AI.
The 2023 Executive Order on AI has already started preparing business leaders for EO-driven regulatory compliance with new and elevated standards for AI safety and security. These new guidelines and guardrails, many of which have deadlines in 2024, will impact investment, AI model development and use.
Rising Fraud Risks
Many online retailers are seeing an increase in fraud, with losses expected to have reached $48 billion in 2023. The 2023 State of Fraud and Financial Crime in North America Annual Report also found that 70% of financial institutions reported that overall fraud rates increased over the past year, an 11% increase from 2022. Phishing remains the top method of fraud, with 43% of online merchants saying that they’ve experienced such an attack, followed closely by friendly/chargeback fraud (34%) and card testing and identity theft, both 33%.
CX can be a line of defense against fraud if the right processes are in place and customer service agents are given the right tools, but as banks, fintechs and retailers grapple with increasing levels of fraud, it’s essential that care is taken not to alienate legitimate customers in the process of fighting it. From call centers to developing e-commerce fraud and retail management programs, organizations should explore ways to protect margins and customer data in ways that foster customer buy-in rather than centering strategies and tactics solely around business needs.
Final Thoughts
As organizations start to hit their stride in 2024, embracing these shifts may mean looking for a trusted partner to outsource some of their business processes. But whether an organization chooses to take this task on themselves or opt for a partner, harmonious integration of new technology and staying on top of risk management and regulatory compliance will be key to sustained success this year and into the future.

title: Council Post: Will 2024 Be The Year AI-Assisted Clinical Decision Support For Doctors Finally Happens?
text:
Dr. Michal Tzuchman-Katz, M.D., CEO and cofounder at Kahun Medical.
In just over 12 months, we've witnessed generative AI (GenAI) become a transformative force across nearly every industry imaginable—including healthcare. Relatively proactive regulations (paywall) have emerged to encourage accountable and ethical AI development as the industry flourishes. One of the most notable steps is President Biden’s benchmark-setting Executive Order geared toward responsible AI development, issued in late October.
That being said, the healthcare industry has taken a noticeably slower, methodical approach to GenAI adoption compared to other fields, even with regulatory strides catalyzing growth in certain sectors. While we did see massive steps in AI-powered administrative assistance, progress in that area alone isn’t enough to truly capture AI’s potential to help providers improve the lives of patients by delivering the highest standard of care.
A recent Google report (paywall), for example, found that its new conversational chatbot had dramatically improved accuracy and empathy compared to physicians. Although the report itself has weaknesses due to the tool not being open for testing and utilizing actors instead of real patients—it does signal concrete progress in an area that healthcare AI builders have been working toward for a decade.
This contradicts reports from groups such as the Advisory Board, who predict that AI-assisted clinical decision support (CDS), including reliable patient diagnosis and treatment plans, is more than four or five years on the horizon. In reality, doctors not only have a growing appetite for these solutions to be available much sooner, but they’re already utilizing general AI tools under the table.
For healthcare AI to continue the momentum of last year’s watershed moment, 2024 must be the year to confidently step into AI-assisted CDS implementation. But there has to be a plan to solve some of GenAI’s lingering issues to ensure the technology matches the demand.
A Status Report On CDS
As AI continues to prove its knack for assisting in administrative tasks, developers have continued to work behind the scenes to get CDS capabilities up to that same level of consistency and specificity.
The problem that plagued 2023, however, was the proliferation of generalized models being stretched beyond their limits. While generative text models (like GPT) are incredibly potent in alleviating administrative burdens, they’re not as apt in the CDS ring precisely due to their broad scope. Since they’re trained on a vast breadth of text, general LLMs have no way to distinguish between factual and non-factual information. That is exacerbated by models not being able to grasp patient-specific data that take their medical history into account.
Additionally, the GenAI industry as a whole continues to grapple with "black box" models that offer no insights into how the output is generated or offer any way to explain itself through evidence. Healthcare was no exception here.
But that "black box" dilemma and its gaps in accuracy or bias don’t necessarily stop physicians from using big-name GenAI tools to help diagnose patients—even if they’re not supposed to. Another problem that arises here is consistency. General AI chatbots are highly sensitive to how questions are prompted to them and can generate widely different responses even to the same prompt that is repeated multiple times.
Taking these gaps into account, what does that mean for the year ahead in CDS advancement?
Making The Year Ahead Impactful
The next year should expand AI-based CDS use to meet the needs of healthcare providers through pilot projects, rigorous testing and even commercialization across inpatient, primary care, specialty care and emergency response facilities. Because, even if physicians are using general chatbots, that doesn’t necessarily mean they fully trust their output.
Building trust requires projects to connect and integrate with private practices, physicians and hospital groups to get up close and personal with doctors in their daily operations. But the key ingredient for that to translate to CDS adoption is through introducing domain-specific models.
The difference between general and domain-specific AI models can be gleaned from the names themselves. If you think of a general large language model like GPT that can be used in broad strokes across many industries, sourcing its information from anywhere, a domain-specific model flips that approach on its head. Rather than building a model to appease everyone, a domain-specific model is specifically tailored not only to a specific industry or subsector but also to where and how it sources its data.
In the medical field, a domain-specific model could be tailored for specialty use and absorb information from anything, including diagnostic reports, patient data, test history or specific medical literature to guide the model in its generative process. In that sense, a domain-specific model gets granular in evidence collection—expanding its potential for specialized use and explainable capabilities to foster CDS.
Aside from domain-specific models leading the charge to increase integrations and pilot projects, we can also expect developers to work on addressing the needs of doctors who could benefit from peer-to-peer consultation or a "co-pilot" to prevent bias or care gaps.
This progress would prove especially powerful for tech-adverse physicians or doctors in rural areas who have limited supportive frameworks. By making CDS well-balanced for these care providers, developers can utilize AI, which is the most intelligent it’s ever been, to consolidate care gaps that might occur.
All these factors explain why 2024 could be a pivotal year for CDS's progress in AI-powered healthcare, as continued integrations, in-field testing and pilot projects will only improve its capabilities.
Of course, much of this potential progress also hinges on regulatory advancements—an aspect that many ethical AI builders have little to no control over. Although last year brought forth impressive regulatory steps in the U.S. and Europe, there is still a disconnect between existing rules and healthcare AI that stresses adoption hesitancy.
To get doctors the tools they are demanding, lawmakers have to set clear compliance boundaries and parameters to ensure AI companies in the healthcare space are commercializing ethical AI. Otherwise, care providers will continue using unsanctioned AI tools that will impede their efficiency and care delivery—further adding to their occupational strain and contributing to declining patient outcomes.

title: AI In The Culinary World: Revolutionizing Restaurant Ops & Customer Experience
text:
The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the restaurant industry is reshaping dining experiences and operational efficiencies. From automating kitchen processes to personalizing customer interactions, AI is enhancing every aspect of the restaurant business. Let’s delve into how restaurants are currently utilizing AI tools and explores potential future applications within the industry.
AI in Customer Service and Interaction
Already, AI is integrated and has significantly improved customer service in restaurants. Chatbots, for instance, are increasingly used for reservations and answering customer questions. Recently, McDonald’s acquired an AI company, Apprente, to integrate voice-based AI technology in its drive-thrus, enabling quicker and more accurate order taking. Similarly, Domino’s Pizza uses an AI assistant, Dom, for online orders, which has streamlined the ordering process and enhanced customer satisfaction. Beyond customer service, AI also plays a role in personalizing dining experiences. Restaurants use AI systems to analyze customer data to offer personalized recommendations and promotions. A notable example is Starbucks' Deep Brew program, which provides tailored suggestions to customers based on their previous purchases and preferences.
AI in Kitchen Operations and Management
In the kitchen, AI is optimizing operations and food preparation. Zume Pizza, for instance, uses AI-driven robots to assist in pizza preparation, improving efficiency and consistency. These robots can spread sauce perfectly and assess cooking times, enhancing the quality of the pizzas. Moreover, inventory management is another area where AI is making significant strides. AI systems predict stock requirements based on historical data and future reservations, helping restaurants avoid overstocking or shortages. A London-based restaurant chain, Dishoom, implemented an AI tool for inventory management that reduced food waste by 20%.
AI in Menu Optimization and Food Design
AI is revolutionizing menu design by analyzing customer preferences and market trends. Machine algorithms suggest menu changes that are likely to appeal to customers, thus driving sales. For instance, a sushi restaurant in Japan, using AI, redesigned its menu based on customer feedback and noticed a 10% increase in customer satisfaction. In food design, AI is helping chefs create novel recipes. IBM’s Chef Watson, an AI system, assists chefs in creating unique recipes by suggesting ingredient combinations that human chefs might not consider. This innovation has led to the creation of novel and popular dishes in several high-end restaurants like the chocolate Austrian burrito and the Vietnamese apple kebob.
AI in Marketing and Customer Analytics
Marketing is another vertical where AI is proving invaluable for the restaurant industry. AI systems analyze customer data to create targeted marketing campaigns. For example, a restaurant chain in the U.S., Chili's, uses AI to analyze customer data and craft personalized marketing messages, leading to increased customer engagement and sales. In conjunction, customer feedback analysis through AI is helping restaurants improve their services. AI algorithms analyze reviews and comments across various platforms to provide actionable insights. TGI Friday’s implemented an AI-driven marketing platform that analyzes customer preferences and feedback, significantly improving their marketing strategy and customer experience.
Future Potential of AI in Restaurants
Looking to the future, AI has the potential to further transform the restaurant industry. Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) are leading the way for immersive dining: Restaurants will use AI with VR/AR to create immersive dining experiences, such as virtual tours of vineyards for wine tastings or thematic dining experiences. Then, there’s the AI-powered personal dietary assistant. Imagine an AI system that analyzes everything you eat… and could eat. These personal dietary assistants would be a huge boon in helping people manage their diet and overall health by suggesting menu items based on individual health goals or dietary restrictions. Next, machines will serve as automated quality control. Restaurants will leverage AI for continuous quality control in the kitchen, ensuring that every dish meets high standards. Additionally, a more traditional use, eateries will use AI for predictive analytics for trend forecasting. AI systems will excel at predicting upcoming culinary trends, helping restaurants stay ahead of the curve in menu development. Finally, our eating experience will have a foundation on robot-assisted dining experiences. Future restaurants could feature AI-driven robots assisting in serving food or even cooking alongside chefs, offering a unique dining experience.
The integration of AI into the restaurant industry is not just a trend but a transformational shift that is redefining dining experiences and operational efficiencies. From enhancing customer service to revolutionizing kitchen operations, AI is a powerful tool in the culinary world. As technology continues to advance, the potential for AI in restaurants is boundless, promising not only improved efficiency and customer satisfaction but also innovative dining experiences. Embracing AI is key for restaurants aiming to stay competitive and offer exceptional services in a rapidly evolving industry.

title: Chip startup Cerebras launches new AI processor - ET Telecom
text:
